notes: Turnout, electors and ballots cast are Elections Canada's figures. Dates are the last polling day.
Seats by party family come from Wikipedia's list of federal elections, regrouped by the families in src/lib/party-families.ts. Green seats come from each election's infobox.

Vote shares are the parties shown in each election's Wikipedia infobox, summed by family; everything else is in 'other'. Before about 1900 many seats were won by acclamation, so vote shares are less comparable.
Majority: the governing party's own seats are at least half the House plus one. Allies (Liberal-Progressives in 1926, Independent Liberals in 1945) aren't counted.

Women elected: the number of women elected at each general election, not counting by-elections, from Wikipedia's list, which counts them three ways; the figure two of them agree on is used. Women couldn't be elected to the House before 1919, so it's 0 before 1921.

elections.note: The House had 181 seats, but no member was returned for Kamouraska, where the election was called off after rioting, so 180 were filled. Many seats were won by acclamation, so vote shares are a rough guide.
Exactly half the seats. Contemporary party labels were loose, and Macdonald governed until the Pacific Scandal in 1873.
A wartime Unionist coalition of Conservatives and pro-conscription Liberals, led by Borden. Counted in the Conservative family.
Exactly the 118 seats needed for a majority. By-elections soon pushed the government in and out of minority.
The Conservatives won more seats, but King's Liberals stayed in office with Progressive support. This led to the King–Byng affair in 1926.
The Liberals had 116 seats; with 8 Liberal-Progressives, who usually voted with them, King had a working majority.
The Liberals had 118 seats, five short, but Independent Liberals gave King a working majority.

elections.turnoutNote: This percentage rises to 70.9 when the number of electors on the lists is adjusted to account for electors who had moved or died between the enumeration for the 1992 referendum and the election of 1993, for which a separate enumeration was not carried out except in Quebec, as the 1992 electoral lists were reused.

The turnout of 61.2% in 2000 was adjusted to arrive at the final turnout of 64.1%, after our normal maintenance of the National Register of Electors to remove the names of deceased electors and duplicates arising from moves. The Chief Electoral Officer of Canada explained the adjustment during his appearance before the Subcommittee on Electoral Boundaries Readjustment on October 6, 2003, and his appearance to discuss the 2004 Main Estimates before the Standing Committee on Procedure and House Affairs on March 5, 2004.

milestones.label: Some women vote
milestones.detail: Women in the armed forces and the female relatives of soldiers get the federal vote for the wartime election.

milestones.label: Women vote on equal terms
milestones.detail: The first general election at which women vote under a universal franchise, after the 1918 and 1920 laws.

milestones.label: Racial exclusions end
milestones.detail: Parliament removes discrimination on the basis of race from the federal franchise, ending the exclusion of Japanese Canadians.

milestones.label: First Nations vote
milestones.detail: First Nations people get the federal vote without having to give up their status under the Indian Act.

milestones.label: Voting age 18
milestones.detail: The voting age drops from 21 to 18, first used at the 1972 election: about two million new electors.

milestones.label: Prisoners vote
milestones.detail: In Sauvé v. Canada the Supreme Court rules that the ban on voting by prisoners serving two years or more is unconstitutional.
